metadata.title: An algebraic approach to virtual fundamental cycles on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves

extraction_notes.note: Sections 1-2 are expository previews of later formal definitions and results (implicit atlas with boundary, product atlas, S^1-equivariant atlas, S^1-localization); per 'one node per repeated statement' these previews got no nodes, only the worked examples and constructions unique to Section 2 did.
Remark environment 'Orbifold fiber product' retyped as an external definition: its content is the (standard, Thurston-cited) definition of the orbifold fiber product.
Single-chart S^1-localization argued in the technical introduction kept as a claim with its prose proof; it is the special case of Theorem 8.6.14 (specializes edge) rather than a restated copy.

The same Convention text is repeated verbatim at the start of Sections 4, 5, 6 (and 8); each scopes its own section, so each is kept as its own assumption node rather than merged as a repeated statement.
Remark environment whose content defines Morse--Smale flow category diagrams; retyped as definition.
Convention environment fixing the ground ring and invertibility of covering-group orders; typed assumption (could be remark).
Definition environment 'Gysin sequence' states the standard Gysin long exact sequence with a justification; typed theorem (external, standard) rather than definition.
Remarks 8.4.9 and 8.7.17 have identical text but sit in different contexts (two different chain models); both kept as separate nodes rather than treated as one repeated statement.
Section 8.4 develops the chain model C^{S^1} in running prose; the list of required properties was taken as one definition node and the spectral-sequence verification as a self-contained remark.
Definition 9.3.14 says it is well-defined by the next lemma, while that lemma uses the defined invariant; to avoid reciprocal uses edges only the definition-to-lemma edge is kept.
Theorem 10.7.24 and the Arnold conjecture corollary are reproofs of results the paper attributes to Liu-Tian, Fukaya-Ono and Ruan, so they are marked external; their proofs are the paper's.
Remark environment whose whole content is an unresolved question (does stalk cohomology imply weak vanishing?); typed open_problem rather than remark.

Theorem B.1.1 parts (i)-(iii) are proved in the proof environment of B.12 and part (iv) in prose in B.13; following 'parts proved separately are claims', each item is a claim nested in the theorem and the proves edges target the parts.

The regular-locus definition and the choice of Q_{0,0} each introduce several auxiliary symbols (B, the bundle, x_i; q_i, V_i, E'', L_0, W) in one construction paragraph; kept as one definition node each.

Appendix C.2 states its main gluing result only as 'the construction of a germ of a local chart' (eq. HFgluinggoal); taken as a prose claim, with the sentence reducing Propositions 10.3.10 and 10.6.21 to it as a prose proof.
The definitions of the cutoff chi and of the torsion T_nabla in C.3/C.5 repeat Appendix B word for word; no prose node here (one node per repeated statement), F880 carries the cutoff formula.
The 'well-known' exponential decay statement in C.1.6 restates Proposition C.11.24 (neckestimateHF); no separate node, the definition of the weights delta_i uses the proposition instead.

Subsection C.12 is a prose continuation of the proof of the Hamiltonian Floer gluing proposition (HFgluingneeded, Prop. 10.3.10) begun earlier in Appendix C; emitted as a separate proof part with a proves edge to that proposition.
Proposition C.11.24 is a known exponential-decay estimate (Floer; proof adapted from Salamon) re-proved here; marked origin external with a paper proof.

Appendix C (Floer gluing) re-introduces its own versions of symbols and terms first defined in Appendix B ($\overline{\mathcal M}$, $C_0$, $j_y$, neck, cylindrical end); defined-term warnings from the B definitions to C nodes were left without edges, since the C nodes rely on their own C definitions.

The symbols $E_I$ and $E_A$ are first introduced inside informal previews in the introduction (no node by the repeated-statement rule); their formal introduction is in Definition 3.1.1, which carries the dependency edges.

metadata.extraction_comment: This 990-environment paper was extracted in nine section-range passes and merged; cross-range defined-term edges were reconciled at merge time, but generic words defined in Appendix A conventions ('space', 'complex', 'support') were deliberately not linked outside that appendix.

nodes.statement: A local chart for X is a diagram: Xar[hookleftarrow]ropen&s_alpha^-1(0)ar[hook]rclosed&X_alphaarrs_alpha&E_alpha where E_alpha is a finite-dimensional vector space (called the obstruction space), X_alpha is an auxiliary moduli space (called the alpha-thickenedfootnotePerhaps a better name would be ``alpha-stabilized moduli space'', though we have decided not to risk confusing this notion of stabilization (i.e.\ product with a vector space) and the notion of stabilizing a Riemann surface (i.e.\ adding marked points). moduli space), and s_alpha is called the Kuranishi map.

nodes.raw_latex: For the purpose of constructing the virtual fundamental cycle of $X$, such a local chart \eqref{localchart} is useful over $X\cap X_\alpha^\mathrm{reg}$, where $X_\alpha^\mathrm{reg}\subseteq X_\alpha$ (called the \emph{regular locus}) is the locus where $X_\alpha$ is cut out transversally (and thus, in particular, $X_\alpha^\mathrm{reg}$ is a finite-dimensional manifold).

nodes.statement: From a theoretical standpoint, it would be desirable to endow the moduli space X with the canonical structure of a ``derived manifold'' (a notion which should be more intrinsic than the notion of an implicit atlas on X). A good notion of a ``derived smooth manifold'' exists (due to Spivak , Borisov--Noel , and Joyce ), and it is reasonable to expect that a parallel topological theory exists as well. By nature, the theory of derived manifolds uses the language of higher category theory. An implicit atlas on X may be thought of as giving a ``presentation'' of X as a derived manifold (just as a collection of open sets of mathbb R^n and gluing data can be used to present an ordinary manifold). The ``atlas'' approach which we follow here, while being less intrinsic, has the advantage of being more concrete and more elementary. We believe that a more intrinsic approach is unlikely to lead to any simplification in the construction of this extra structure (implicit atlas or derived manifold structure) on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves. However, it would likely make it easier to work with (and, in particular, calculate) virtual fundamental cycles on such spaces.

nodes.statement: The language of infty-categories as developed by Lurie seems to be a natural setting for the VFC package and, more generally, for a good theory of derived manifolds and their virtual fundamental cycles (indeed, the existing theory of derived smooth manifolds is by necessity written in the language of higher category theory). We have avoided infty-categories in this paper for sake of concreteness (though at the cost of needing to use lots of explicit homotopy colimits). However, we expect that in this more abstract framework, one could ultimately develop the most flexible calculational tools (computing virtual fundamental cycles directly from our defintion seems rather difficult, due to the inexplicit nature of the isomorphism ).

nodes.statement: The requirement that X_I be a manifold whenever I is nonempty is rather unnatural (c.f.\ Remark ) and is too strong of an assumption for two different reasons. First, we do not know how to construct implicit atlases with this property on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves (it is a subtle question of choosing good neighborhoods to ensure transversality over all X_I if \#Igeq 1). Second, with this axiom we cannot form the ``product implicit atlas'' (Definition ) which is crucial for understanding coherence of virtual fundamental cycles between moduli spaces when treating Floer-type homology theories. Thus in the real definition of an implicit atlas (Definition ), there is no such requirement on X_I. The requirement that $X_I$ be a manifold \emph{whenever $I$ is nonempty} is rather unnatural (c.f.\ Remark \ref{Iemptynotspecial}) and is too strong of an assumption for two different reasons.  First, we do not know how to construct implicit atlases with this property on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves (it is a subtle question of choosing good neighborhoods to ensure transversality over all $X_I$ if $\#I\geq 1$).  Second, with this axiom we cannot form the ``product implicit atlas'' (Definition \ref{productimplicitatlas}) which is crucial for understanding coherence of virtual fundamental cycles between moduli spaces when treating Floer-type homology theories.  Thus in the real definition of an implicit atlas (Definition \ref{implicitatlasdefinition}), there is no such requirement on $X_I$.  Rather, we specify open subsets $X_I^\mathrm{reg}\subseteq X_I$ for all $I\subseteq A$ (morally, this is the locus where $X_I$ is cut out transversally), and we modify the transversality axioms appropriately.

nodes.statement: The most natural notion of ``equivalence'' between two implicit atlases A and B on a space X seems to be the existence of a chain of inclusions of implicit atlases Asubseteq C_1supseteqcdotssubseteq C_nsupseteq B. It is common to speak of ``cobordisms'' between Kuranishi structures or Kuranishi atlases; the analogous notion of cobordism between implicit atlases (say on the same index set A) on a space X is an implicit atlas with boundary on Xtimes[0,1] whose restriction to the boundary coincides with the first (resp.\ second) implicit atlas on Xtimes\0\ (resp.\ Xtimes\1\). It is an easy consequence of the VFC machinery that the virtual fundamental class is invariant under both notions of equivalence.

nodes.name: Orbifold fiber product
nodes.statement: Let mathcal X,mathcal Y,mathcal Z be orbifolds, and fix maps of orbifolds mathcal X,mathcal Ytomathcal Z. Then the orbifold fiber product mathcal Xtimes_mathcal Zmathcal Y is simply the categorical 2-fiber product in the weak 2-category of orbifolds. It exists whenever mathcal Xtimesmathcal Ytomathcal Ztimesmathcal Z is transverse to the diagonal mathcal Ztomathcal Ztimesmathcal Z (in particular, it exists if at least one of the maps mathcal X,mathcal Ytomathcal Z is \'etale as in the above example of X_alphato X). Thurston gives an explicit hands-on definition of mathcal Xtimes_mathcal Zmathcal Y in the case mathcal X,mathcal Ytomathcal Z are both \'etale by working locally on mathcal Z and then gluing. In a more modern perspective (defining orbifolds as certain stacks on the site of smooth manifolds), we may define the orbifold fiber product by the following universal property: Hom(S,mathcal Xtimes_mathcal Zmathcal Y):=Hom(S,mathcal X)times_Hom(S,mathcal Z)Hom(S,mathcal Y) for any smooth manifold S. The right hand side denotes the 2-fiber product in the weak 2-category of groupoids, which admits the explicit description: G_1times_HG_2:=Bigl\(g_1,g_2,theta)Bigm|g_1in G_1,\,g_2in G_2,\,theta\!:\!f_1(g_1)to f_2(g_2)Bigr\ (with the obvious notion of isomorphism between triples (g_1,g_2,theta)) for groupoids G_1,G_2,H and functors f_i:G_ito H. The orbifold fiber product usually does not coincide with the fiber product of the underlying topological spaces Xtimes_YZ, though there is at least always a map mathcal Xtimes_mathcal Zmathcal Yto Xtimes_ZY. The construction would not work if we used the fiber product of topological spaces.

nodes.statement: The reader may rightfully object that the index set A defined above is not a set but rather a groupoid (just as there is no ``set of all finite sets'' or ``set of all compact smooth manifolds''). There are two ways of resolving this issue. The simplest solution is to add appropriate ``rigidifying data'' to turn A into a set (e.g.\ we could add the data of an isomorphism E_alphaxrightarrowsimmathbb R^dim E_alpha to the definition of a thickening datum). Another (more cumbersome, and ultimately unnecessary) solution would be to just check that the notion of an implicit atlas and the accompanying theory of virtual fundamental cycles remains valid for A a groupoid instead of a set (see also Remark for more details).

nodes.statement: The thickened moduli spaces overlinemathcal M_0,0(X,B)_I are defined as moduli spaces of solutions to the ``I-thickened barpartial-equation'' . With this intrinsic definition, the convenient overlap properties of the charts (the compatibility axioms) follow rather trivially. The atlas also clearly does not depend on any choice of Sobolev norms or ``gluing profile''. On this point, it is useful to compare with other approaches, which often take the perspective of defining thickened moduli spaces as subsets of some particular Banach manifold of maps. In this context, achieving good overlap properties seems to be more difficult and less conceptual. Another inconvenience of this setting is the lack of differentiability of the reparameterization action (and large reparameterization groups for bubbles).

nodes.statement: Standard gluing techniques suffice to verify the openness and submersion axioms for the implicit atlases we construct on moduli spaces of pseudo-holomorphic curves. In fact, the transition maps between gluing charts are clearly smooth when restricted to each stratum (i.e.\ for a fixed topological type of the domain), and this yields a canonical ``stratified smooth structure'' on each X_I^reg. If one wanted to obtain a smooth structure on the X_I^reg, one would need to construct gluing charts whose transition maps are truly smooth. This would require a choice of ``gluing profile'' (on which the resulting smooth structure would depend) and is slightly more delicate (see Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono or Hofer--Wysocki--Zehnder ). Such methods might yield smooth implicit atlases (see Definition ).

nodes.statement: There are many different choices for what one could mean by a ``compatible system of implicit atlases'' mathcal A(p,q) on the spaces mathcal X(p,q). For sake of exposition, we have chosen here the structure for which it is easiest to apply the VFC package. In the actual construction in S, we use the structure which is the easiest to construct in practice (via the natural generalization of S). As a result, various complexes that here coincide are only canonically quasi-isomorphic in S. Basically, this means that in S, we will have to take lots of homotopy colimits to make certain maps well-defined on the chain level. A systematic use of infty-categories of complexes would tame the resulting explosion of notation, at the cost of relying on that more abstract language/machinery.

nodes.statement: A natural strategy for proving S^1-localization results is to consider X_I/S^1 as forming an atlas on X/S^1 of virtual dimension one less, and then ``pulling back'' to X the virtual fundamental cycle on X/S^1 (this is the approach taken by Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono ). In the general setting where the S^1-action is merely continuous, the implicit atlas on X does not induce an implicit atlas on X/S^1 because of the existence of free S^1-actions on topological manifolds whose quotients are not manifoldsfootnoteSuch an action may be constructed out of any non-manifold X for which Xtimesmathbb R is a manfold (namely the obvious action on Xtimes S^1). Many examples of such spaces are known, the first being due to Bing ; see also Cannon ., though we still consider this ``quotient implicit atlas'' in spirit. This extra generality is convenient, since it means we do not need to construct an S^1-equivariant gluing map (providing the local slice necessary to show that the ``quotient implicit atlas'' exists).

nodes.name: Using finite $I\to A$ instead of finite $I\subseteq A$
nodes.statement: An implicit atlas consists of data parameterized by the category of finite subsets of A (objects: finite subsets, morphisms: inclusions). A direct modification of the definition allows one to instead use the category of finite sets over A (objects: finite sets Ito A, morphisms: injective maps Ihookrightarrow J compatible with the maps to A). In fact, all constructions of implicit atlases we know of yield implicit atlases in this generalized sense. We won't need this generalization in this paper, but let us point out some reasons why it may be useful to keep in mind. With the definition as it stands now (using finite subsets of A), we can ``pull back'' an implicit atlas along any injection Bhookrightarrow A. If we instead use finite sets over A, then we can pull back an implicit atlas along any map Bto A (in fact, we can pull back along any coproduct preserving functor from finite sets over B to finite sets over A, which amounts to the specification of a finite set I_betato A for all betain B). Also, in the category of finite subsets of A we can only take the disjoint union of subsets which are already disjoint; however in the category of finite sets over A there exist arbitrary abstract finite disjoint unions. This allows some extra (though currently unneeded) flexibility in certain constructions, since we do not need to ensure certain sets are disjoint or that certain maps are injective. Using the category of sets over A is also the natural perspective to take if we wanted to allow A to be a groupoid instead of a set (then an object is a finite set I along with a collection of objects \alpha_i\_iin I of A, and a morphism (I,\alpha_i\_iin I)to(J,\alpha_j\_jin J) is an injection j:Ihookrightarrow J along with isomorphisms alpha_ixrightarrowsimalpha_j(i) in A).

\label{bettertouseovercategory}
An implicit atlas consists of data parameterized by the \emph{category of finite subsets of $A$} (objects: finite subsets, morphisms: inclusions).  A direct modification of the definition allows one to instead use the \emph{category of finite sets over $A$} (objects: finite sets $I\to A$, morphisms: injective maps $I\hookrightarrow J$ compatible with the maps to $A$).  In fact, all constructions of implicit atlases we know of yield implicit atlases in this generalized sense.  We won't need this generalization in this paper, but let us point out some reasons why it may be useful to keep in mind.

With the definition as it stands now (using finite subsets of $A$), we can ``pull back'' an implicit atlas along any \emph{injection} $B\hookrightarrow A$.  If we instead use finite sets over $A$, then we can pull back an implicit atlas along any \emph{map} $B\to A$ (in fact, we can pull back along any \emph{coproduct preserving functor} from finite sets over $B$ to finite sets over $A$, which amounts to the specification of a finite set $I_\beta\to A$ for all $\beta\in B$).  Also, in the category of finite subsets of $A$ we can only take the disjoint union of subsets which are already disjoint; however in the category of finite sets over $A$ there exist arbitrary abstract finite disjoint unions.  This allows some extra (though currently unneeded) flexibility in certain constructions, since we do not need to ensure certain sets are disjoint or that certain maps are injective.

Using the category of sets over $A$ is also the natural perspective to take if we wanted to allow $A$ to be a groupoid instead of a set (then an object is a finite set $I$ along with a collection of objects $\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in I}$ of $A$, and a morphism $(I,\{\alpha_i\}_{i\in I})\to(J,\{\alpha_j\}_{j\in J})$ is an injection $j:I\hookrightarrow J$ along with isomorphisms $\alpha_i\xrightarrow\sim\alpha_{j(i)}$ in $A$).

\label{IAorientationsheaf}
Let $X$ be a space with locally orientable implicit atlas $A$ with boundary.  Then there exists a sheaf $\mathfrak o_{X,A}$ on $X$ equipped with $\Gamma_I$-equivariant isomorphisms $\psi_{\varnothing I}^\ast\mathfrak o_{X,A}\xrightarrow\sim\mathfrak o_{X_I^\mathrm{reg}}\otimes\mathfrak o_{E_I}^\vee$ over $(s_I|X_I^\mathrm{reg})^{-1}(0)$ for every $I\subseteq A$, which are compatible with the maps $\psi_{IJ}$. nodes.name: Chains and cochains
nodes.statement: We use C_bullet(X) (resp.\ C^bullet(X)) to denote singular simplicial chains (resp.\ cochains) on a space X, and we use C_bullet(X,Y) to denote the cokernel of C_bullet(Y)hookrightarrow C_bullet(X) for Ysubseteq X (``relative chains''). Let us also recall the ``Eilenberg--Zilber map'' C_bullet(X)otimes C_bullet(Y)to C_bullet(Xtimes Y) for spaces X and Y, corresponding to the standard subdivision of Delta^ntimesDelta^m into binomn+mn copies of Delta^n+m. The Eilenberg--Zilber map is associative (in the sense that it gives rise to a unique map C_bullet(X)otimes C_bullet(Y)otimes C_bullet(Z)to C_bullet(Xtimes Ytimes Z)) and commutative (in the sense that the following diagram commutes: C_bullet(X)otimes C_bullet(Y)@>>>C_bullet(Xtimes Y)cr @VVV@VVVcr C_bullet(Y)otimes C_bullet(X)@>>>C_bullet(Ytimes X) for all X and Y). We should point out that this commutativity fails for some other common models of singular chains, for example singular cubical chains (modulo degeneracies).

nodes.name: Independence of chain model
nodes.statement: The particular choice of singular simplicial chains is not particularly important. The virtual fundamental classes, etc.\ resulting from our theory should be unchanged by using any other model of singular chains. This independence would follow immediately (and all issues about finding chain models with good chain level functoriality properties would go away) if we setup the VFC package using infty-categories.

nodes.name: Comparison of homology theories
nodes.statement: There are (at least) three natural ``homology groups'' which one can assign to a compact Hausdorff space X: itemDual of v Cech cohomology check H^bullet(X)^vee (^vee denotes dual, i.e.\ Hom(-,R)). itemv Cech homology check H_bullet(X) (the inverse limit of the homology of nerves of finite covers). itemSteenrod--Sitnikov homology overline H_bullet(X) (the homology of the homotopy/derived inverse limit of nerves of finite covers; see S). These are successively more refined, in the sense that there are natural maps: overline H_bullet(X)tocheck H_bullet(X)tocheck H^bullet(X)^vee If X is homeomorphic to a finite CW-complex, then there are natural isomorphisms: overline H_bullet(X)=H_bullet(X) check H_bullet(X)=H_bullet(X) check H^bullet(X)^vee=H^bullet(X)^vee It follows that a virtual fundamental class in any of these groups can be used for all the applications we are aware of. On the other hand, there are some potential advantages to working with the more refined homology groups: itemoverline H_bullet and check H_bullet retain torsion information. itemoverline H_bullet and check H_bullet have a natural ``extension of scalars'' map for any map of rings Rto S. itemoverline H_bullet has the expected long exact sequence for pairs of spaces.

nodes.name: {Calculating $[X]^\mathrm{vir}$ using perturbation}
nodes.statement: The properties from this section can be used to calculate the virtual fundamental class in the following sense. Let us suppose we are given an ``explicit'' implicit atlas A on a space X. We may always (for convenience) replace A by a subatlas and/or shrink the charts of A and the virtual fundamental class is preserved (Lemmas and ). Now suppose we can extend A to an implicit atlas with boundary on a space Y with partial Y=Xcup X' where X'=(X')^reg (if A is a smooth implicit atlas, then such an extension is obtained if one can ``coherently perturb'' the Kuranishi maps s_alpha so they become transverse to zero). Then X' is a closed smooth manifold, and [X']^vir=[X'] is the naive fundamental class (Lemma ). Now Y is a cobordism between X and X', so we have [X]^vir=[X'] as homology classes in Y (Lemmas and ). This allows us to understand the pushforward of [X]^vir under any map f:Xto Z which extends continuously to Y. We do not claim such perturbations always exist; an affirmative answer is provided in very similar, though not identical, contexts by Fukaya--Ono , Fukaya--Oh--Ohta--Ono and McDuff--Wehrheim .

\label{perturbationcalc}
The properties from this section can be used to calculate the virtual fundamental class in the following sense.  Let us suppose we are given an ``explicit'' implicit atlas $A$ on a space $X$.  We may always (for convenience) replace $A$ by a subatlas and/or shrink the charts of $A$ and the virtual fundamental class is preserved (Lemmas \ref{sameassubatlas} and \ref{openreduction}).  Now suppose we can extend $A$ to an implicit atlas with boundary on a space $Y$ with $\partial Y=X\cup X'$ where $X'=(X')^\mathrm{reg}$ (if $A$ is a smooth implicit atlas, then such an extension is obtained if one can ``coherently perturb'' the Kuranishi maps $s_\alpha$ so they become transverse to zero).  Then $X'$ is a closed smooth manifold, and $[X']^\mathrm{vir}=[X']$ is the naive fundamental class (Lemma \ref{fclasstransverse}).  Now $Y$ is a cobordism between $X$ and $X'$, so we have $[X]^\mathrm{vir}=[X']$ as homology classes in $Y$ (Lemmas \ref{disjointunionfc} and \ref{cobordismworks}). Let $\tau_E\in H^k(E,E\setminus 0;p^\ast\mathfrak o_E)$ denote the Thom class of $E$ (characterized uniquely by the property that its restriction to any local trivialization $\mathbb R^n\times U\to U$ is the pullback of the tautological class in $H^n(\mathbb R^n,\mathbb R^n\setminus 0;\mathfrak o_{\mathbb R^n})$).

The \emph{Euler class} $e(E)\in H^k(B;\mathfrak o_E)$ is $s^\ast\tau_E$ where $s:B\to E$ is any section.  Any two sections are homotopic, so $e(E)$ is well-defined. The natural map $H^k_c(B;\mathfrak o_E)\to H^k(B;\mathfrak o_E)$ sends the Euler class with compact support to the Euler class.

Since $\mathfrak s\prec\mathfrak t$, we have $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq M^{<\mathfrak t}=\partial M^{\leq\mathfrak t}$, giving (\ref{inbdry}).

Recall Brouwer's ``invariance of domain'', which implies that if a subset $X\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is (in the subspace topology) locally homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^m$, then $m\leq n$, with equality iff $X$ is open.  This immediately gives (\ref{toplessdim}), (\ref{topopen}).

We prove (\ref{bdrystratumstruct}).  Fix $p\in M^\mathfrak s$.  A neighborhood of $p$ is covered by strata $\succ\mathfrak s$, so since $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq M$ is not open, there exists a stratum $\mathfrak t\succ\mathfrak s$.  Now $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq\partial M^{\leq\mathfrak t}$ is open by (\ref{topopen}) (applied to $M^{<\mathfrak t}\to\mathcal S^{<\mathfrak t}$).  A doubling argument (and invariance of domain) near $p\in\partial M$ shows that $M^s\cup M^\mathfrak t$ contains a neighborhood of $p$.  Since we have exhausted a neighborhood of $p\in M^\mathfrak s$, it follows using (\ref{inbdry}) that there is no other stratum $\succ\mathfrak s$.

We prove (\ref{intstratumstruct}).  Fix $p\in M^\mathfrak s$.  A neighborhood of $p$ is covered by strata $\succ\mathfrak s$, so since $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq M$ is not open, there exists a stratum $\mathfrak t\succ\mathfrak s$.  Now $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq\partial M^{\leq\mathfrak t}$ is open by (\ref{topopen}), as is $M^\mathfrak t\subseteq M$.  This gives a collar on one side of $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq M$.  This still does not fill out a neighborhood of $p$, so there exists $\mathfrak t'\ne\mathfrak t$ with $\mathfrak t'\succ\mathfrak s$, giving a collar on the other side of $M^\mathfrak s\subseteq M$.  Now by invariance of domain, we have thus exhausted a neighborhood of $p\in M^\mathfrak s$ inside $M$, and hence it follows using (\ref{inbdry}) that there are no more strata $\succ\mathfrak s$ other than $\mathfrak t,\mathfrak t'$.

nodes.statement: As a first step towards understanding the main construction of this section, let us first describe a similar construction in a more familiar setting. Let M be a topological manifold with cell-like stratification by mathcal S. Define: C_bullet(M;mathcal S):=bigoplus_mathfrak sinmathcal SC_bullet-(dim M-dimmathfrak s)(M^leqmathfrak s;mathfrak o_Motimesmathfrak o_M^leqmathfrak s^vee) equipped with the differential given by the sum over codim(mathfrak spreceqmathfrak t)=1 of the pushforwards C_bullet(M^leqmathfrak s)to C_bullet(M^leqmathfrak t) (covered by the dual of the boundary map mathfrak o_M^leqmathfrak ttomathfrak o_M^leqmathfrak s) plus the internal differential. This differential squares to zero by Lemma (the square of the differential is a sum over codim(mathfrak spreceqmathfrak t)=2 of maps C_bullet(M^leqmathfrak s)to C_bullet(M^leqmathfrak t), each of which can be seen to vanish by applying Lemma () to M^<mathfrak ttomathcal S^<mathfrak t). Now there is a natural map: C_bullet(M;mathcal S)&to C_bullet(M)\\ bigoplus_mathfrak sinmathcal Sgamma_mathfrak s&mapstosum_mathfrak sinmathcal Scrdimmathfrak s=dim Mgamma_mathfrak s (it follows from Lemma that this is a chain map) which we claim is a quasi-isomorphism. To see that is a quasi-isomorphism, observe that it is the map on global sections of a corresponding map of complexes of mathcal K-presheaves C_bullet(M,Msetminus K;mathcal S)to C_bullet(M,Msetminus K) on the one-point compactification M_+ of M. Both are homotopy mathcal K-sheaves by Lemma . Thus by Corollary , it suffices to show that the map C_bullet(M,Msetminus p;mathcal S)to C_bullet(M,Msetminus p) is a quasi-isomorphism for every pin M. This holds by the following local argument. Note that H_bullet(M,Msetminus p;mathcal S) is isomorphic to mathbb Z (to see this, consider the filtration by dimmathfrak s), so it suffices to construct a cycle in C_bullet(M,Msetminus p;mathcal S) representing a generator of mathbb Z and show that its image in H_bullet(M,Msetminus p)=mathbb Z is a generator. Such a cycle may be constructed by induction on mathcal S (starting from the stratum containing p and going up), and its image in H_bullet(M,Msetminus p) generates since its degree at p coincides with its degree at any nearby point in an open stratum, which is one by construction. A similar argument appears in Barraud--Cornea . Thus we can think of C_bullet(M;mathcal S) as a model for chains on M (the reader should make sure they understand what this means geometrically).

nodes.statement: If one is satisfied with working in the homotopy category (i.e.\ constructing a diagram Z_bulletto H^0(Ch_R)), then one needs only the 2-skeleton of Z_bullet. On the other hand, there is little simplification to be gained by using 2-truncated semisimplicial sets instead of semisimplicial sets. If one is satisfied with working in the homotopy category (i.e.\ constructing a diagram $Z_\bullet\to H^0(\mathsf{Ch}_R)$), then one needs only the $2$-skeleton of $Z_\bullet$. Moreover, the ``higher homotopies'' which are kept track of in $\mathsf{N}_{\mathsf{dg}}(\mathsf{Ch}_R)$ are known to contain interesting information in certain settings (for example, they can be used to obstruct isotopies between symplectic embeddings, as in Floer--Hofer--Wysocki \cite{floerhoferwysockiSHI}).

nodes.name: Simplicial set and semisimplicial set
nodes.statement: Let Delta be the category of finite nonempty totally ordered sets with morphisms weakly order-preserving maps. Let Delta_inj be the subcategory of injective morphisms. A simplicial set Z_bullet is a functor Z:Delta^optoSet, and a semisimplicial set Z_bullet is a functor Z:Delta_inj^optoSet. In both cases, we write Z_n for Z(\0,ldots,n\). For sigmain Z_n and 0leq j_0<cdots<j_mleq n, we denote by sigma|[j_0ldots j_m] the image of sigma under the map Z_nto Z_m induced by the map \0,ldots,m\to\0,ldots,n\ given by imapsto j_i (sigma|[j_0ldots j_m] is called a facet of sigma); if m=0 we also write sigma(j) for sigma|[j].
nodes.raw_latex: Let $\Delta$ be the category of finite nonempty totally ordered sets with morphisms weakly order-preserving maps.  Let $\Delta_\mathrm{inj}$ be the subcategory of injective morphisms.  A \emph{simplicial set} $Z_\bullet$ is a functor $Z:\Delta^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}$, and a \emph{semisimplicial set} $Z_\bullet$ is a functor $Z:\Delta_\mathrm{inj}^\mathrm{op}\to\mathsf{Set}$.  In both cases, we write $Z_n$ for $Z(\{0,\ldots,n\})$.  For $\sigma\in Z_n$ and $0\leq j_0<\cdots<j_m\leq n$, we denote by $\sigma|[j_0\ldots j_m]$ the image of $\sigma$ under the map $Z_n\to Z_m$ induced by the map $\{0,\ldots,m\}\to\{0,\ldots,n\}$ given by $i\mapsto j_i$ ($\sigma|[j_0\ldots j_m]$ is called a facet of $\sigma$); if $m=0$ we also write $\sigma(j)$ for $\sigma|[j]$.

It is equivalent to show that given any $f:\Delta^n\to Z_\bullet$ along with data (\ref{subatlaschoice})--(\ref{augmentationschoice}) over $\partial\Delta^n$, the data can be extended over $\Delta^n$.  For ease of notation, let us rename $(f^\ast\mathcal X,f^\ast\mathcal A,f^\ast\omega)$ as $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\omega)$.

We construct (\ref{subatlaschoice})--(\ref{augmentationschoice}) via $H$-equivariant induction on the set of triples $(\sigma,p,q)$, equipped with the partial order $\preceq_\mathcal X$ in which $(\sigma',p',q')\preceq_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ iff $(\sigma',p',q')$ appears as a ``factor'' of some element of $\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$.  This partial order is \emph{well-founded} (i.e.\ there is no strictly decreasing infinite sequence) since each $\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ is finite, and thus it is valid for induction.  The induction works $H$-equivariantly since the action of $H$ on $\mathcal P$ is free, and $(\sigma,p,q)$ and $(\sigma,hp,hq)$ are always incomparable for $h\in H$ (so we may henceforth ignore the action of $H$).  The inductive step is as follows.

\textbf{Choosing $\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)$.}\  We must choose a finite $\bar\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)\subseteq\bar\mathcal A(\sigma,p,q)$ so that the corresponding subatlas of $\mathcal A(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}}=\bar\mathcal A(\sigma,p,q)$ on $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ satisfies the covering axiom (and thus is an implicit atlas).  This is possible by compactness.

\textbf{Choosing $[E_\alpha]$.}\  Trivial.

\textbf{Choosing $[[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}:QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z(\sigma,p,q)\to\mathbb Z$.}\  We need to construct $[[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}$ fitting into the following diagram:
\begin{equation}
\label{choosingEEdiagram}\begin{tikzcd}[column sep = huge]
\smash{\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}}QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak s)\ar[tail]{r}{\text{product/face}}\ar{d}[swap]{[[E]]}&QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z(\sigma,p,q)\ar[dashed]{dl}{?\exists\,[[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}}\\
\mathbb Z\\
H_\bullet\smash{\displaystyle\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{\mathfrak s\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}}QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak s)\ar{r}{\text{product/face}}\ar{d}[swap]{[[E]]}&H_\bullet QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z(\sigma,p,q)\ar{dl}{[E]\mapsto 1}\\
\mathbb Z
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
Since $QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z$ is cofibrant, it follows that the top horizontal map is a cofibration between cofibrant complexes (this uses Lemma \ref{cofibranthaslotsofcofibrations}).  Now Lemma \ref{Hzeroofcofibrantcolimit} tells us that the direct sum of $H_0QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+_\mathbb Z(\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak s)$ surjects onto $H_0$ on the left, and this makes it easy to check that the second diagram commutes.  Lemma \ref{Hzeroofcofibrantcolimit} also tells us that $H_{-1}$ on the left vanishes.  Hence we may apply Lemma \ref{cocycleextendinglemma} to conclude the existence of a suitable $[[E]]_{\sigma,p,q}$.

\textbf{Choosing $\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ (the key step).}\  According to Lemma \ref{mappingconechoiceboundary}, we may choose a $\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ with the required property iff the homology class of $\mu_{\sigma,p,q}\in H^\bullet_\mathrm{vir}(\partial\mathcal X;\mathcal B)^+(\sigma,p,q)$ coincides with $d\omega(\sigma,p,q)\in\check H^0(\partial\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q);\mathfrak o_{\partial\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)})$.  Let us now prove this desired statement $[\mu_{\sigma,p,q}]=d\omega(\sigma,p,q)$.  Let us fix $\mathfrak r_0\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ and verify equality over $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\mathfrak r_0}$ (this is clearly enough).

We consider the following diagram:
\begin{align}
\label{mucareabout}\mu_{\sigma,p,q}\in&&&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X;\mathcal B)^+(\sigma,p,q)\\
&&&\qquad\uparrow\cr
\label{muallstrat}\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}\in&&\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{\mathfrak s\prec\mathfrak t\in\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r}}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak s}\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak t})\\
&&&\qquad\downarrow\cr
\label{musomestrat}\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}\in&&\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{\mathfrak s\prec\mathfrak t\in\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r}}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak s}\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak t})\\
&&&\qquad\uparrow\cr
\label{muonestratum}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r_0}\in&&\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}_{\mathfrak s\prec\mathfrak t\in\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak s}\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak t})
\end{align}
The differentials in \eqref{muallstrat}--\eqref{musomestrat} are given by the sum over $\operatorname{codim}(\mathfrak r\preceq\mathfrak r')=1$ of the obvious pushforward maps (plus the internal differentials of each $\operatornamewithlimits{hocolim}$).  The first vertical map is the sum over $\operatorname{codim}\mathfrak r=0$ (i.e.\ over maximal elements of $\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$); clearly this is a chain map.  The remaining vertical maps are clear.  The easiest way to keep track of signs in the present discussion is to use the orientation lines associated to elements of $\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$, as in Definition \ref{stratifiedvirtualdef}, though we will supress them from the notation.  Note that there is a natural diagram of complexes of $\mathcal K$-presheaves on $\partial\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ whose diagram of global sections is \eqref{mucareabout}--\eqref{muonestratum}.  We will see below that these complexes of $\mathcal K$-presheaves are in fact pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves and that the induced diagram of sheaves (obtained by taking $H^0$) is given by the tautological maps:
\begin{equation}\label{orientationdiagramforHFbdry}
\mathfrak o_{\partial\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\leftarrow\mathfrak o_{\partial\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\to\mathfrak o_{\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}\leftarrow\mathfrak o_{\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}\operatorname{rel}\partial}
\end{equation}
First, though, let us argue that this claim implies the desired result.  The cycle $\mu_{\sigma,p,q}\in\eqref{mucareabout}$ lifts to a cycle $\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}\in\eqref{muallstrat}$, where $\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}$ is obtained by applying the product/face maps to the tensor product of the various $\lambda$'s corresponding to the factors on the left hand side of \eqref{Wtotalcomposition} corresponding to $\mathfrak r$ (this is a cycle by \eqref{lambdamaster}).  Obviously $\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}\in\eqref{muallstrat}$ maps to $\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}\in\eqref{musomestrat}$.  On sections over $K\subseteq\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\mathfrak r_0}$, the last vertical map is an isomorphism, and (the restriction to $K$ of) $\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r}\in\eqref{musomestrat}$ lifts to (the restriction to $K$ of) $\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r_0}\in\eqref{muonestratum}$.  Finally, observe that over any $K\subseteq\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\mathfrak r_0}$, the homology class of $\mu_{\sigma,p,q,\mathfrak r_0}\in\eqref{muonestratum}$ coincides with the restriction of $d\omega(\sigma,p,q)$ to the $\mathfrak r_0$ stratum (this follows from the induction hypothesis, using the fact that the orientations are coherent and the observation at the end of Definition \ref{productatlasF}).  Clearly this implies that $\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$ coincides with $d\omega(\sigma,p,q)$ in homology over $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\mathfrak r_0}$.

Thus it remains only to show that \eqref{mucareabout}--\eqref{muonestratum} are pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves and that the induced maps on $H^0$ coincide with the tautological maps on orientation sheaves \eqref{orientationdiagramforHFbdry}.  Note that by Proposition \ref{stratifiedispurehomotopysheaf}, the following closely related diagram satisfies all of the desired properties (i.e.\ is a diagram of pure homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves inducing \eqref{orientationdiagramforHFbdry} on $H^0$):
\begin{align}
&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\partial\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q);\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}})\\
&\qquad\uparrow\cr
\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r}\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}})\\
&\qquad\downarrow\cr
\bigoplus_{\mathfrak r\in\partial\mathcal S_\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}}&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r}\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}})\\
&\qquad\uparrow\cr
&C_\mathrm{vir}^\bullet(\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^{\leq\mathfrak r_0}\operatorname{rel}\partial;\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}})
\end{align}
Hence it is enough to relate this diagram to \eqref{mucareabout}--\eqref{muonestratum} via quasi-isomorphisms.  The diagram obtained from \eqref{mucareabout}--\eqref{muonestratum} by replacing every occurence of $\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak t}$ with $\mathcal B(\sigma,p,q)^{\geq\mathfrak s^\mathrm{top}}$ maps quasi-isomorphically to \eqref{mucareabout}--\eqref{muonestratum} (by pairing with the fixed fundamental cycles), and it also maps quasi-isomorphically to the diagram above (use the obvious pushforwards on the $p=0$ level of the homotopy colimits, and zero for $p>0$), thus giving the desired result.

\textbf{Choosing $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$.}\  We must find $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ lifting $s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ and satisfying $d\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}=\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$.  Now we know that $\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$ is a cycle (see Definition \ref{systemofcycles}); furthermore its image in $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+$ is $s_\ast\mu_{\sigma,p,q}=d(s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q})$ which is null-homologous.  Since $Q\mathcal W_\bullet\overset\sim\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal W_\bullet$ is always a quasi-isomorphism, it follows that $\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$ is null-homologous.  Hence there exists $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'$ with $d\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'=\tilde\mu_{\sigma,p,q}$; now we must modify $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'$ so that it lifts $s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$.  The difference of $s_\ast\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}$ and the image of $\tilde\lambda_{\sigma,p,q}'$ is a cycle in $C_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+$.  It can be lifted to a cycle in $QC_\bullet(E;\mathcal B)^+$ using Lemma \ref{cycleliftinglemma} (again using that $Q\mathcal W_\bullet\overset\sim\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal W_\bullet$ is a quasi-isomorphism), which is enough.

nodes.name: Novikov rings
nodes.statement: Let T be a set equipped with a ``grading'' gr:Ttomathbb Z and an ``action'' a:Ttomathbb R. We let R[[T]] denote the graded R-module consisting of formal sums sum_tin Tc_tcdot t with c_tin R, satisfying the following two finiteness conditions: item\#\ninmathbb Z:exists t such that c_tne 0 and gr(t)=n\<infty. item\#\tin T:c_tne 0 and a(t)<M\<infty for all M<infty. In other words, R[[T]] is the graded completion of R[T] with respect to the non-archimedean a-adic norm left|tright|_a:=e^-a(t). If T is a group and gr, a are group homomorphisms, then R[[T]] is a graded ring.

nodes.statement: Apply the Tietze extension theorem to the identity map S^1pto S^1p to obtain an S^1-invariant neighborhood K of S^1p and a retraction r:Kto S^1p. By averaging and passing to a smaller neighborhood, we may assume without loss of generality that r is S^1-equivariant. Now by the naturality of the Euler class, we have e(K)=r^ast e(S^1p). Thus it suffices to show that e(S^1p)in H^2_S^1(S^1p) vanishes. Now we have H^2_S^1(S^1p)=H^2_(S^1)_p(p)=H^2((S^1)_p), where the latter is the group cohomology of the finite stabilizer group (S^1)_p. It is a standard fact that the group cohomology of a finite group is annihilated by the order of the group. Hence our assumption that \#(S^1)_p is invertible in R guarantees that this cohomology group vanishes.

nodes.raw_latex:
A \emph{PL manifold with cells} $(M,\mathcal S)$ is a compact connected nonempty orientable PL-manifold with boundary $M$ with stratification by a finite poset $\mathcal S$ (see Definition \ref{stratificationdefinition}) such that:
\begin{rlist}
\item$M^{\leq\mathfrak s}$ is a connected nonempty orientable PL-submanifold with boundary.
\item$(M^{\leq\mathfrak s})^\circ=M^\mathfrak s$.
\item$\mathcal S$ has a unique maximal element.
\end{rlist}
For every $\mathfrak s\in\mathcal S$, there corresponds a \emph{face} $(M^{\leq\mathfrak s},\mathcal S^{\leq\mathfrak s})$, which is also a PL manifold with cells.

nodes.statement: An MF-set is a set mathcal Y along with: item For every iinmathcal Y, a PL manifold with cells (M_i,mathcal S_i). item(Face identifications). For every iinmathcal Y and every mathfrak sinmathcal S_i, an index jinmathcal Y and an isomorphism (M_i^leqmathfrak s,mathcal S_i^leqmathfrak s)xrightarrowsim(M_j,mathcal S_j). These indices and isomorphisms must be (strictly) transitive in the following obvious sense. If mathfrak sinmathcal S is maximal, then j=i and (M_i,mathcal S_i)=(M_i^leqmathfrak s,mathcal S_i^leqmathfrak s)xrightarrowsim(M_j,mathcal S_j)=(M_i,mathcal S_i) is the identity map. If mathfrak s'preceqmathfrak s is a nested pair of faces with identifications (M_i^leqmathfrak s,mathcal S_i^leqmathfrak s)xrightarrowsim(M_j,mathcal S_j) and (M_i^leqmathfrak s',mathcal S_i^leqmathfrak s')xrightarrowsim(M_j',mathcal S_j'), and the mathfrak s' face of (M_j,mathcal S_j) is identified (M_j^leqmathfrak s',mathcal S_j^leqmathfrak s')xrightarrowsim(M_k,mathcal S_k), then k=j' and the two identifications of (M_i^leqmathfrak s',mathcal S_i^leqmathfrak s') with (M_k,mathcal S_k)=(M_j',mathcal S_j') are the same. A morphism of MF-sets f:mathcal Ytomathcal Y' is a map of sets covered by isomorphisms (M_i,mathcal S_i)to(M_f(i),mathcal S_f(i)), compatible with the face identifications for mathcal Y and mathcal Y' in the obvious way. The category of MF-sets has a natural symmetric monoidal structure: given MF-sets \M_i\_iinmathcal Y and \M_j'\_jinmathcal Y', their product is defined to be \M_itimes M_j'\_(i,j)inmathcal Ytimesmathcal Y', which is again an MF-set. For an MF-set mathcal Y, let C^mathcal Y_bullet(X) denote the complex freely generatedfootnoteA given map M_ito X contributes a copy of the orientation module of M_i, which is isomorphic to mathbb Z but not canonically so. by maps M_ito X (for iinmathcal Y), with differential given by the obvious sum over all codimension one faces. Note that there is a natural map: C_bullet^mathcal Y(X)otimesmathcal C_bullet^mathcal Y'(X')to C_bullet^mathcal Ytimesmathcal Y'(Xtimes X')

Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, there exists a morphism of MF-sets $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ (where $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is as in Example \ref{standardsimplicialMFset}).  Since $C_\bullet(X)=C^{\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}}_\bullet(X)$ by definition, we obtain a chain map $C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)$.  The resulting map:
\begin{equation}\label{homologyYcomparison}
H_\bullet(X)\to H_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)
\end{equation}
is independent of the choice of morphism $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$, as can be seen as follows.  There is an MF-set $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\times[0,1]\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ where each $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ is as in Example \ref{standardsimplicialMFset}, where $\Delta^n\times[0,1]$ is given the product stratification ($[0,1]$ stratified by $\{\{0\},\{1\},(0,1)\}$), and $\Delta^n\times\{0\}$ (resp.\ $\Delta^n\times\{1\}$) is identified with the first (resp.\ second) copy of $\Delta^n$.  Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, it follows that for any pair of morphisms $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ there is a morphism $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\times[0,1]\}_{n\geq 0}\sqcup\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ whose restriction to the two copies of $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$ are the two given morphisms.  From this data one easily constructs a chain homotopy between the two maps $C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)$.  Hence the map \eqref{homologyYcomparison} is canonical.

Now let us show that \eqref{homologyYcomparison} is an isomorphism.  Fix a map $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$.  Fix triangulations $T_i$ of $M_i$ for which each $M_i^{\leq\mathfrak s}$ is a union of simplices, which are compatible with the face identifications, and which restrict to the tautological triangulation of $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}$.  Such triangulations may be constructed by induction.  By triangulation, we mean a triangulation in which each simplex is equipped with a total order on its set of vertices, compatible with its faces (i.e.\ a semisimplicial set rather than a simplicial complex).  Such triangluations induce a map of complexes $C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_\bullet(X)$, and the composition $C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_\bullet(X)$ is clearly the identity map.  It suffices to show that the other composition is chain homotopic to the identity map.

Now let us define a new MF-set in terms of the map $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ and the triangulations $T_i$.  Note that the stratification of $M_i$ by the face poset $\mathcal F(T_i)$ of $T_i$ refines the stratification by $\mathcal S_i$; in other words we have maps $M_i\to\mathcal F(T_i)\to\mathcal S_i$.  The objects of the new MF-set are $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$, where $M_i\times[0,1]$ is stratified by the following strata:
\begin{align}
M_i^\mathfrak s\times\{0\}&\quad\mathfrak s\in\mathcal S_i\\
M_i^\mathfrak s\times(0,1)&\quad\mathfrak s\in\mathcal S_i\\
M_i^\mathfrak t\times\{1\}&\quad\mathfrak t\in\mathcal F(T_i)
\end{align}
Thus the poset of strata of $M_i\times[0,1]$ is $\mathcal S_i\sqcup\mathcal S_i\sqcup\mathcal F(T_i)$.  For the face identifications, $M_i\times\{0\}$ is identified tautologically with $M_i$, and each of the closed strata $M_i^{\leq\mathfrak t}\times\{1\}$ ($\mathfrak t\in\mathcal F(T_i)$) is identified with the corresponding $\Delta^n$ (considered as an object of $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ via the inclusion $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$).

Now we have a chain of inclusions $\{\Delta^n\}_{n\geq 0}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\hookrightarrow\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$.  Since $\mathcal Y$ is saturated, there in fact exists a map backwards $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\sqcup\{M_i\times[0,1]\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}\to\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$ (acting identically on $\{M_i\}_{i\in\mathcal Y}$).  Using this map, we obtain a chain map $C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_{\bullet+1}^\mathcal Y(X)$ (precompose chains with the projection $M_i\times[0,1]\to M_i$).  This map is a chain homotopy between the identity map and the composition $C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)\to C_\bullet(X)\to C_\bullet^\mathcal Y(X)$, so we are done.

\label{saturatedcalculatesHSS}
Let $\mathcal Y$ be a saturated $S^1$-MF-set.  Then there is a canonical isomorphism between $S^1$-equivariant singular homology $H^{S^1}_\bullet(X)$ and $H^{S^1,\mathcal Y}_\bullet(X)$ (the homology of $C^{S^1,\mathcal Y}_\bullet(X)$).  Furthermore, the natural map $C_\bullet^{S^1,\mathcal Y}(X)\to C_{\bullet+1}^{\mathcal Y'}(X)$ induces the Gysin map on homology, for $\mathcal Y'$ a saturated MF-set.

nodes.statement: All S^1-MF-sets in this proof will share the same (ES^1)_mathcal Yto(BS^1)_mathcal Y, so we will omit the subscript _mathcal Y from the notation. Let \Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1 denote the S^1-MF-set indexed by pairs (n,f) consisting of an integer ngeq 0 and a PL map f:Delta^nto BS^1, where the stratifications and face identifications are as in Example . Now the complex C^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X) is freely generated by maps Delta^nto(Xtimes ES^1)/S^1 whose composition with the projection (Xtimes ES^1)/S^1to BS^1 is PL. A straightforward approximation argument shows that the inclusion of this complex into the complex generated by all maps Delta^nto(Xtimes ES^1)/S^1 is a quasi-isomorphism. Hence there is a canonical isomorphism: H^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X)xrightarrowsim H_bullet((Xtimes ES^1)/S^1)=H_bullet^S^1(X) As in the proof of Lemma there exists a morphism of S^1-MF-sets \Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1tomathcal Y since mathcal Y is saturated. This induces a chain map C^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X)to C^S^1,mathcal Y_bullet(X), which as before induces a canonical map on homology: H^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X)to H^S^1,mathcal Y_bullet(X) which is independent of the choice of morphism \Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1tomathcal Y. It suffices to show that this map is an isomorphism. Fix a map \Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1tomathcal Y, which we observe is necessarily injective. Fix triangulations T_i of M_i as in the proof of Lemma . Such triangulations induce a map of complexes C^S^1,mathcal Y_bullet(X)to C^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X). The composition C^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X)to C^S^1,mathcal Y_bullet(X)to C^S^1,\Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1_bullet(X) is clearly the identity map. It thus suffices to show that the reverse composition is chain homotopic to the identity. As in the proof of Lemma , we construct a new S^1-MF-set, namely \M_i\_iinmathcal Ysqcup\M_itimes[0,1]\_iinmathcal Y, from the inclusion \Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1hookrightarrow\M_i\_iinmathcal Y and the triangulations T_i. There are inclusions \Delta^n\_ngeq 0,f:Delta^nto BS^1hookrightarrow\M_i\_iinmathcal Yhookrightarrow\M_i\_iinmathcal Ysqcup\M_itimes[0,1]\_iinmathcal Y. The desired chain homotopy may then be constructed as in the proof of Lemma . The fact that the induced map H^S^1_bullet(X)to H_bullet+1(X) is the Gysin map is left to the reader.

\label{circlelocalizationhomology}
Let $\mathcal X/Z_\bullet$ be an $H$-equivariant flow category diagram with implicit atlas $\mathcal A$ and coherent orientations $\omega$, satisfying the hypotheses of Definition \ref{defofhomologygroups}.  Suppose that $S^1$ acts compatibly on this entire structure ($S^1$-actions on $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)$ and $S^1$-equivariant implicit atlases, so that all the relevant structure maps are $S^1$-equivariant).

Fix partitions (into disjoint closed subsets):
\begin{equation}\label{partitionsfreefixedII}
\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)=\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^0\sqcup\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^1
\end{equation}
where $S^1$ acts almost freely on $\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^1$, and suppose that the product/face maps specialize to maps:
\begin{align}
\label{PFfirst}\mathcal X(\sigma|[0\ldots k],p,q)^0\times\mathcal X(\sigma|[k\ldots n],q,r)^0&\to\mathcal X(\sigma,p,r)^0\\
\mathcal X(\sigma|[0\ldots k],p,q)^0\times\mathcal X(\sigma|[k\ldots n],q,r)^1&\to\mathcal X(\sigma,p,r)^1\\
\mathcal X(\sigma|[0\ldots k],p,q)^1\times\mathcal X(\sigma|[k\ldots n],q,r)^0&\to\mathcal X(\sigma,p,r)^1\\
\mathcal X(\sigma|[0\ldots k],p,q)^1\times\mathcal X(\sigma|[k\ldots n],q,r)^1&\to\mathcal X(\sigma,p,r)^1\\
\label{PFface}\mathcal X(\sigma|[0\ldots\hat k\ldots n],p,q)^0&\to\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^0\\
\label{PFlast}\mathcal X(\sigma|[0\ldots\hat k\ldots n],p,q)^1&\to\mathcal X(\sigma,p,q)^1
\end{align}
Assume in addition that for any vertex $\sigma^0\in Z_\bullet$, we have $\mathcal X(\sigma^0,p,q)^0=\varnothing\implies\mathcal X(\sigma^i,p,q)^0=\varnothing$ for all $i$ and $p\ne q$.

Then there is a canonical isomorphism $\mathbb H(\mathcal X)_\mathcal A=\mathbb H(\mathcal X^0)_\mathcal A$, where $\mathcal X^0$ is the $H$-equivariant flow category diagram with product/face maps given by \eqref{PFfirst} and \eqref{PFface}, equipped with the implicit atlas obtained by removing $\mathcal X^1$ from every thickening.

nodes.name: Nodal curve of type $(g,n)$
nodes.statement: A nodal curve of type (g,n) is a compact nodal Riemann surface C of arithmetic genus g along with an injective function l:\1,ldots,n\to C (the ``n marked points'') whose image is disjoint from the nodes of C. An isomorphism (C,l)to(C',l') of curves of type (g,n) is an isomorphism of Riemann surfaces iota:Cto C' such that l'=iotacirc l. We usually omit l from the notation. Such a curve is called stable iff its automorphism group is finite.
nodes.raw_latex: A \emph{nodal curve of type $(g,n)$} is a compact nodal Riemann surface $C$ of arithmetic genus $g$ along with an injective function $l:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to C$ (the ``$n$ marked points'') whose image is disjoint from the nodes of $C$.  An \emph{isomorphism $(C,l)\to(C',l')$ of curves of type $(g,n)$} is an isomorphism of Riemann surfaces $\iota:C\to C'$ such that $l'=\iota\circ l$.  We usually omit $l$ from the notation.  Such a curve is called \emph{stable} iff its automorphism group is finite.

nodes.name: $J$-holomorphic map
nodes.statement: A J-holomorphic map of type (g,n) is a pair (C,u) where C is a nodal curve of type (g,n) and u:Cto X is smooth and satisfies barpartial u=0. An isomorphism (C,u)to(C',u') of J-holomorphic maps of type (g,n) is an isomorphism iota:Cto C' of curves of type (g,n) such that u=u'circiota. We say a J-holomorphic map is stable iff its automorphism group (i.e.\ group of self-isomorphisms) is finite.
nodes.raw_latex: A \emph{$J$-holomorphic map of type $(g,n)$} is a pair $(C,u)$ where $C$ is a nodal curve of type $(g,n)$ and $u:C\to X$ is smooth and satisfies $\bar\partial u=0$. We say a $J$-holomorphic map is \emph{stable} iff its automorphism group (i.e.\ group of self-isomorphisms) is finite.

A \emph{(Gromov--Witten) thickening datum} $\alpha$ is a 6-tuple $(D_\alpha,r_\alpha,\Gamma_\alpha,\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha,E_\alpha,\lambda_\alpha)$ where:
\begin{rlist}
\item$D_\alpha\to X$ is a compact smooth embedded codimension two submanifold with boundary.
\item$r_\alpha\geq 0$ is an integer such that $2g+n+r_\alpha>2$.
\item$\Gamma_\alpha$ is a finite group.
\item$\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha$ is a smooth $\Gamma_\alpha$-manifold\footnote{Note that we do not assume $\Gamma_\alpha$ acts effectively on $\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha$.  Indeed, $\overline{\mathcal M}_{1,1}$ and $\overline{\mathcal M}_{2,0}$ are ineffective orbifolds, so we must allow ineffective actions if we want $\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha/\Gamma_\alpha$ to be isomorphic to an open subset of one of these spaces.} equipped with an isomorphism of orbifolds between $\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha/\Gamma_\alpha$ and an open subset of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n+r_\alpha}/S_{r_\alpha}$ (let $\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\to\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha$ be the pullback\footnote{Pullback here means the orbifold fiber product (see Remark \ref{orbifoldfiberproductrmk}).  Note that the fibers of $\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\to\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha$ are nodal curves of type $(g,n+r_\alpha)$ (not quotiented by their automorphism group).} of the universal family; the action of $\Gamma_\alpha$ on $\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha$ lifts canonically to $\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha$ by the universal property of the pullback).
\item$E_\alpha$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb R[\Gamma_\alpha]$-module.
\item$\lambda_\alpha:E_\alpha\to C^\infty(\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\times X,\Omega^{0,1}_{\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha/\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha}\otimes_\mathbb C TX)$ is a $\Gamma_\alpha$-equivariant linear map supported away from the nodes and marked points of the fibers of $\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha\to\overline{\mathcal M}_\alpha$.
\end{rlist}

nodes.name: Transversality of smooth maps
nodes.statement: Let u:Cto X be a smooth map from a nodal curve of type (g,n), and let Dsubseteq X be a smooth codimension two submanifold with boundary. We say u is transverse to D (written upitchfork D) iff u^-1(partial D)=0 and forall\,pin u^-1(D), the derivative du:T_pCto T_u(p)X/T_u(p)D is surjective and p is neither a node nor a marked point of C.

Equip $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,n}^\beta(X)_I$ with the Gromov topology\footnote{When $I\ne\varnothing$, this topology is easy to define: it is simply given by using the Hausdorff distance on the image $C\subseteq X\times\prod_{\alpha\in I}\overline{\mathcal C}_\alpha$.} for $(u,\phi_\alpha)$ and with the obvious topology for $e_\alpha$. nodes.name: Standard Morse function on $\Delta^n$
nodes.statement: For this definition, let us view the n-simplex Delta^n as: Delta^n=\underline xin[0,1]^n+1:0=x_0leqcdotsleq x_nleq 1\ The ith vertex of Delta^n is given by x_n-i=0 and x_n-i+1=1. We now consider the Morse function on Delta^n given by f(x):=sum_i=1^ncospi x_i. Its gradient: nabla f(x)=sum_i=1^npisin(pi x_i)fracpartialpartial x_i is tangent to the boundary of Delta^n, and its critical points are precisely the vertices of Delta^n, the index at vertex i being n-i. Note also that for any facet inclusion Delta^khookrightarrowDelta^n, the pushforward of nabla f is again nabla f. Let us consider the space mathcal F(Delta^n) of broken Morse flow lines from vertex 0 (index n) to vertex n (index 0). This space is homeomorphic to a cube [0,1]^n-1, the factors [0,1] being naturally indexed by the ``middle vertices'' 1,ldots,n-1 of Delta^n. A flow line is broken at a vertex iin\1,ldots,n-1\ iff the corresponding coordinate in [0,1]^n-1 equals 1. Note that for any simplex sigma there are canonical compatible product/face maps: mathcal F(sigma|[0ldots k])timesmathcal F(sigma|[kldots n])&tomathcal F(sigma)\\ mathcal F(sigma|[0ldotshat kldots n])&tomathcal F(sigma) See also S for more details. We define a $\pi$-equivariant flow category diagram $\overline{\mathcal M}/J\!H_\bullet(M)$ as follows.
\begin{rlist}
\item For a vertex $(J,H)\in J_0(M)\times H_0(M)$, we let $\mathcal P_{(J,H)}=\mathcal P_H$.

\item The action $a:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R$ is the usual symplectic action, and $a:\pi\to\mathbb R$ is given by $a(h)=\langle\omega,h\rangle$.
\item We let $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)$ be the set of stable Floer trajectories of type $(\sigma,p,q)$, equipped with the Gromov topology.  It is well-known that $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)$ is compact Hausdorff.  The finiteness conditions required on $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)$ also follow from Gromov compactness.  The product/face maps on $\overline{\mathcal M}(\sigma,p,q)$ are evident.
\item The action of $\pi$ on everything is clear.
\end{rlist}

This is a standard yet tricky exercise.  We recall one of the (many) standard proofs.

The map $\phi$ is described by some matrix of $A\times B$ elements of $R$.  Certainly the kernel of this matrix remains zero over the subring of $R$ generated by its entries.  Thus we may assume without loss of generality that $R$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-algebra.  Now localize at a prime ideal $\mathfrak p\subset R$ of height zero.  Localization is exact, so again $\phi$ remains injective.  Thus we may assume without loss of generality that $R$ is a local Noetherian ring of dimension zero, and thus $R$ is an Artin local ring \cite[p90, Theorem 8.5]{atiyahmacdonald}.  Since $R$ is Artinian, all finitely generated modules have finite length \cite[pp76--77, Propositions 6.5 and 6.8]{atiyahmacdonald}, and hence there is a length homomorphism $K_0(R)\to\mathbb Z$ \cite[p77, Proposition 6.9]{atiyahmacdonald} (which is clearly an isomorphism since $R$ is local).  It thus follows from the short exact sequence $0\to R^{\oplus A}\xrightarrow\phi R^{\oplus B}\to\operatorname{coker}\phi\to 0$ that $A\leq B$.

nodes.statement: A refinement of a cover \U_alpha\_alphain A is a cover \U_beta\_betain B along with a map f:Bto A such that U_betasubseteq U_f(alpha). Refinements are the morphisms used in the directed systems used to define (all flavors of) v Cech cohomology. Different refinements \U_alpha\_alphain Ato\U_beta\_betain B induce different maps on v Cech complexes, but they all agree after passing to cohomology (more precisely, the ``space'' of such refinements is contractible or empty). \label{coveringscategoryrmk}
A \emph{refinement} of a cover $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}$ is a cover $\{U_\beta\}_{\beta\in B}$ along with a map $f:B\to A$ such that $U_\beta\subseteq U_{f(\alpha)}$.  Refinements are the morphisms used in the directed systems used to define (all flavors of) \v Cech cohomology.  Different refinements $\{U_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in A}\to\{U_\beta\}_{\beta\in B}$ induce different maps on \v Cech complexes, but they all agree after passing to cohomology (more precisely, the ``space'' of such refinements is contractible or empty).  In particular, it follows that the directed systems used in defining \v Cech cohomology are \emph{filtered}.

nodes.name: Why homotopy $\mathcal K$-sheaves instead of homotopy sheaves?
nodes.statement: The naive modification of substituting open Usubseteq X in place of compact Ksubseteq X does not yield a homotopy sheaf. To get a homotopy sheaf, one could apply the proposed functor Ralpha_ast:hShv_mathcal K XtohShv X from Remark to the homotopy mathcal K-sheaf . It is somewhat easier, though, to just work directly in the setting of homotopy mathcal K-sheaves (which has some advantages, for example stalks of mathcal K-presheaves are easier to define/understand). It is for this reason that throughout this paper we work with homotopy mathcal K-sheaves instead of homotopy sheaves.

\end{align}

nodes.statement: The operator D_alpha,y equals (nablaxi)^0,1_y plus compact terms (by Lemma ), so it is equivalent to show that ximapsto(nablaxi)^0,1_y is Fredholm (and we may forget about E). Here nabla is really the pullback of nabla via u_alpha. Thus it suffices to show that if V is a smooth complex vector bundle over a nodal Riemann surface C equipped with a smooth connection nabla, then the horizontal maps: [column sep = large] W^k,2,delta(C,V)arrximapsto(nablaxi)^0,1&W^k-1,2,delta(tilde C,Omega^0,1_tilde Cotimes_mathbb C V)\\ W^k,2(C,V)ar[hook]uarrximapsto(nablaxi)^0,1&W^k-1,2(tilde C,Omega^0,1_tilde Cotimes_mathbb C V)ar[hook]u are Fredholm. For the bottom map, the Fredholm property is standard. Indeed, W^k,2(C,V) lies inside W^k,2(tilde C,V) as a closed subspace of finite codimension, and nabla^0,1:W^k,2(tilde C,V)to W^k-1,2(tilde C,Omega^0,1_tilde Cotimes_mathbb C V) is Fredholm by elliptic regularity on the compact Riemann surface tilde C. For the top map, the Fredholm property follows from results of Lockhart--McOwen concerning the Fredholmness (in weighted Sobolev spaces) of elliptic operators on manifolds with cylindrical ends. Specifically, W^k,2,delta(C,V) lies inside W^k,2,delta(tilde C,V) as a closed subspace of finite codimension, and the map nabla^0,1:W^k,2,delta(tilde C,V)to W^k-1,2,delta(tilde C,Omega^0,1_tilde Cotimes_mathbb C V) is Fredholm by the theory of Lockhart--McOwen . This uses the fact that the weight deltain(0,1) is not an eigenvalue of the asymptotic linearized operator in any end (the set of eigenvalues in any end is precisely mathbb Z, corresponding to the powers \z^n\_ninmathbb Z on D^2setminus 0). Let us also remark that both of these Fredholmness statements are easier at p=2 than for general pin(1,infty), since for p=2 one can use Fourier analysis (after localizing the problem with a partition of unity). Now it remains to show that the induced maps on kernel and cokernel are isomorphisms. The map on kernels is obviously injective, and the map on cokernels is easily seen to be surjective (use the fact that the image of the top horizontal map is closed and the fact that the rightmost vertical inclusion is dense). For the surjectivity of the map on kernels and the injectivity of the map on cokernels, it suffices to show that if D_alpha,yxi=eta for xiin W^k,2,delta and etain W^k-1,2, then xiin W^k,2. Certainly (the vector field part of) xi extends continuously to C_alpha (by definition of W^k,2,delta), and this continuous extension satisfies D_alpha,yxi=eta+epsilon where epsilon is a distribution on tilde C_alpha valued in Omega^0,1_tilde C_alpha,j_yotimes_mathbb C u_alpha^ast TX and supported inside the (inverse images of the) nodes. On the other hand, epsilon is supported at a finite set of points, so it is a linear combination of delta-functions and their derivatives. This gives rise to the bottom right vertical map in . We define the middle vertical maps in using parallel transport (equivalently, using the local trivializations defined by ). Let $(\alpha_i,y_i,u_i,\{x^i_j\},e_i)\in\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$ be a sequence converging to $(0,0,u_0,\{x^0_j\},e_0)$.  We must show that for $i$ sufficiently large, $(\alpha_i,y_i,u_i,\{x^i_j\},e_i)$ is contained in the image of the map \eqref{gluingmap}.  We may restrict to sequences rather than nets since the topology on $\overline{\mathcal M}(X)$ is first countable (recall the definition of the topology following \eqref{Mbarfirstdef}; it is even a metric topology).  This is convenient when we apply Arzel\`a--Ascoli.

Let us define $\xi_i\in C^\infty(C_{\alpha_i},u_{\alpha_i}^\ast TX)_D\oplus E$ by the property:
\begin{align}
u_i&=\exp_{u_{\alpha_i}}\xi_i\\
e_i&=e_0+\operatorname{proj}_E\xi_i
\end{align}
(and the exponential follows the shortest geodesic).  Obviously $\operatorname{proj}_E\xi_i\to 0$ and $\left\|\xi_i\right\|_\infty\to 0$.

Now we claim that $u_i\to u$ in the $C^\infty$ topology away from the nodes, or equivalently, that $\xi_i\to 0$ in the $C^\infty$ topology away from the nodes of $C_0$.  To see this argue as follows.  The thickened holomorphic curve equation from \eqref{modulispace} is equivalent to an honest holomorphic curve equation for the graph $u:C\to C\times X$ where the almost complex structure on $C\times X$ is defined in terms of $\lambda(e)$.  Hence the Gromov--Schwarz Lemma (see \cite[p316, 1.3.A]{gromov} or \cite[p223, Corollary 4.1.4]{muller}) applies and we conclude that $\left\|du_i\right\|_\infty$ is uniformly bounded, on compact sets away from the nodes (equivalently, the same for $\left\|d\xi_i\right\|_\infty$).  Now elliptic bootstrapping (as in the proof of Lemma \ref{Woneinftycontrolsall}) implies that all derivatives are bounded uniformly on compact sets away from the nodes.  Using Arzel\`a--Ascoli and diagonalization, we conclude that there exists a subsequence of $u_i$ which is convergent in the $C^\infty$ topology away from the nodes.  Since we know that $u_i\to u$ in the $C^0$ topology, the limit of this $C^\infty$ convergent subsequence must be $u$.  This argument can be applied to any subsequence of $u_i$, so we conclude that every subsequence of $u_i$ has a subsequence which converges to $u$ in $C^\infty$ away from the nodes.  It follows that in fact $u_i$ itself converges to $u$ in $C^\infty$ away from the nodes.

In the ends/necks of $C_{\alpha_i}$, note that $u_i$ is genuinely $J$-holomorphic (the $\lambda$ term vanishes), so we may apply Proposition \ref{neckestimate} to conclude that $\left\|\xi_i\right\|_{k,2,\delta}\to 0$ (here using the fact that $\delta<1$).  We should remark that to apply Proposition \ref{neckestimate}, we need to be able to choose some $M<\infty$ such that for any neck $[0,6S]\times S^2\subseteq C_{\alpha_i}$, the derivatives of $u_i$ restricted to $\partial[M,6S-M]\subseteq C_{\alpha_i}$ are bounded by $\delta$ (the constant in Proposition \ref{neckestimate}).  Such an $M$ exists because of our earlier observation that $u_i\to u$ in $C^\infty$ on compact sets away from the nodes, and we can certainly choose a large $M$ such that the derivatives of $u$ over $\{M\}\times S^1\subseteq[0,\infty)\times S^1\subseteq C_0$ (any end) are arbitrarily small.

Let us define $\kappa_i\in K$ by the property that $\xi_i\in(\kappa_i)_{\alpha_i}+\operatorname{im} Q_{\alpha_i,y_i}$.  Now since $\left\|\xi_i\right\|_{k,2,\delta}\to 0$ and the norms on the left and right of \eqref{QKtoall} are uniformly commensurable, we see that $\kappa_i\to 0$.  Now the uniqueness in Proposition \ref{newtoniteration} shows that $\xi_i=(\kappa_i)_{\alpha_i,y_i}$ for $i$ sufficiently large.  Thus we are done.

nodes.statement: Let B(1)subseteqmathbb R^n denote the closed unit ball and B(1)^circ its interior. We know that f(B(1)) is compact (since f is continuous) and Hausdorff (since X is Hausdorff). We know that f:B(1)to f(B(1)) is bijective (since f is injective), so it is in fact a homeomorphism. Now choose an open subset Vsubseteq X with f(0)in Vsubseteq f(B(1)^circ) (which exists by assumption). Set U=f^-1(V)cap B(1)^circ, which is clearly open. Now f:Uto f(U) is a homeomorphism onto its image (since Usubseteq B(1)), and f(U)=V is open.

Let $B(1)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ denote the closed unit ball and $B(1)^\circ$ its interior.  We know that $f(B(1))$ is compact (since $f$ is continuous) and Hausdorff (since $X$ is Hausdorff).  We know that $f:B(1)\to f(B(1))$ is bijective (since $f$ is injective), so it is in fact a homeomorphism.

Now choose an open subset $V\subseteq X$ with $f(0)\in V\subseteq f(B(1)^\circ)$ (which exists by assumption).  Set $U=f^{-1}(V)\cap B(1)^\circ$, which is clearly open.  Now $f:U\to f(U)$ is a homeomorphism onto its image (since $U\subseteq B(1)$), and $f(U)=V$ is open.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{weightedonespace}
We define the weighted Sobolev space $W^{k,2,\delta,\delta}(C_\alpha,u_\alpha^\ast TM)$ using the usual $(k,2)$-norm away from the ends/necks, and using the following weighted $(k,2)$-norms over the bubble ends/necks and main ends/necks respectively (we will write the contribution to the norm squared):
\begin{align}
\label{endnormHFbubble}\left|\xi(n)\right|^2+&\int_{S^1\times[0,\infty)}\biggl[\left|\xi(t,s)-\xi(n)\right|^2+\sum_{j=1}^k\left|D^j\xi(t,s)\right|^2\biggr]e^{2\delta s}\;dt\,ds\\
\label{necknormHFbubble}\biggl|\int_{S^1}\xi(t,3S)\,dt\biggr|^2+&\int_{S^1\times[0,6S]}\biggl[\Bigl|\xi(t,s)-\int_{S^1}\xi(t,3S)\,dt\Bigr|^2+\sum_{j=1}^k\left|D^j\xi(t,s)\right|^2\biggr]e^{2\delta\min(s,6S-s)}\;dt\,ds\\
\label{endnormHFmain}&\int_{S^1\times[N,\infty)}\sum_{j=0}^k\left|D^j\xi(t,s)\right|^2e^{2\delta(s-N)}\;dt\,ds\\
\label{necknormHFmain}&\int_{S^1\times[N,6S-N]}\sum_{j=0}^k\left|D^j\xi(t,s)\right|^2e^{2\delta\min(s-N,6S-N-s)}\;dt\,ds
\end{align}
These are to be interpreted as follows.  For each bubble node $n\in C_0$, we fix, once and for all, a small trivialization of $TM$ in a neighborhood of $u_0(n)$; this allows us to view $\xi$ as a function (rather than a section) for the purposes of the integrals over the bubble ends/necks.  For each $i=0,\ldots,k$, we fix, once and for all, a smooth family of trivializations of $TM$ near $\gamma_i(t)$ (parameterized by $t\in S^1$); this allows us to view $\xi$ as a section of $\gamma_i^\ast TM$ for the purposes of the integrals over the main ends/necks.  We also fix, once and for all, a connection on each such bundle $\gamma_i^\ast TM$ over $S^1$.  The derivatives in the integrals above are measured with respect to the standard metric on $S^1\times\mathbb R$.  The case of negative main ends is completely analogous to that of positive main ends.  

By Sobolev embedding $W^{2,2}\hookrightarrow C^0$ in two dimensions, we get uniform bounds linear in $\left\|\xi\right\|_{k,2,\delta,\delta}$ on $\left|\xi(t,s)-\xi(n)\right|e^{\delta s}$ in the bubble ends, $\left|\xi(t,s)\right|e^{\delta s}$ in the main ends, and $\left|D^j\xi(t,s)\right|e^{\delta s}$ ($1\leq j\leq k-2$) in all ends (as well as similar estimates in the necks).

We will occasionally use other very similar weighted Sobolev spaces (e.g.\ $W^{k,2,\delta,\delta}(C_0,u_{0|\alpha}^\ast TM)$), and we leave it to the reader to make the necessary adjustments to the definition (which is essentially identical to the above).
nodes.clean_text: We define the weighted Sobolev space W^k,2,delta,delta(C_alpha,u_alpha^ast TM) using the usual (k,2)-norm away from the ends/necks, and using the following weighted (k,2)-norms over the bubble ends/necks and main ends/necks respectively (we will write the contribution to the norm squared): left|xi(n)right|^2+&int_S^1times[0,infty)biggl[left|xi(t,s)-xi(n)right|^2+sum_j=1^kleft|D^jxi(t,s)right|^2biggr]e^2delta s\;dt\,ds\\ biggl|int_S^1xi(t,3S)\,dtbiggr|^2+&int_S^1times[0,6S]biggl[Bigl|xi(t,s)-int_S^1xi(t,3S)\,dtBigr|^2+sum_j=1^kleft|D^jxi(t,s)right|^2biggr]e^2deltamin(s,6S-s)\;dt\,ds\\ &int_S^1times[N,infty)sum_j=0^kleft|D^jxi(t,s)right|^2e^2delta(s-N)\;dt\,ds\\ &int_S^1times[N,6S-N]sum_j=0^kleft|D^jxi(t,s)right|^2e^2deltamin(s-N,6S-N-s)\;dt\,ds These are to be interpreted as follows. For each bubble node nin C_0, we fix, once and for all, a small trivialization of TM in a neighborhood of u_0(n); this allows us to view xi as a function (rather than a section) for the purposes of the integrals over the bubble ends/necks. For each i=0,ldots,k, we fix, once and for all, a smooth family of trivializations of TM near gamma_i(t) (parameterized by tin S^1); this allows us to view xi as a section of gamma_i^ast TM for the purposes of the integrals over the main ends/necks. We also fix, once and for all, a connection on each such bundle gamma_i^ast TM over S^1. The derivatives in the integrals above are measured with respect to the standard metric on S^1timesmathbb R. The case of negative main ends is completely analogous to that of positive main ends. By Sobolev embedding W^2,2hookrightarrow C^0 in two dimensions, we get uniform bounds linear in left\|xiright\|_k,2,delta,delta on left|xi(t,s)-xi(n)right|e^delta s in the bubble ends, left|xi(t,s)right|e^delta s in the main ends, and left|D^jxi(t,s)right|e^delta s (1leq jleq k-2) in all ends (as well as similar estimates in the necks). We will occasionally use other very similar weighted Sobolev spaces (e.g.\ W^k,2,delta,delta(C_0,u_0|alpha^ast TM)), and we leave it to the reader to make the necessary adjustments to the definition (which is essentially identical to the above).
